title: Cue, routine, reward
hookLine: brain research on rats in mazes, and the popular cue-routine-reward loop
carry: the cue is where a habit can be seen
last: THE SOUL IS DYED BY WHAT WE REPEAT.

lines: A CLICK. A GATE. A RAT RUNS.
cards: A click. A gate slides open at the bottom of a small maze, and a rat runs. At the end of the run, if it turns the right way, there's a bit of chocolate.
The first few times, the rat sniffs, hesitates, wanders. With enough practice it runs the route like it's on rails.
That small scene, played out in neuroscience labs, sits underneath a loop that has since spread through books, podcasts and office walls: cue, routine, reward.
Today starts with the first word of that loop, and asks what the lab actually saw.

teach.b: First, the lab. Neuroscientist Ann Graybiel and her team recorded activity in a deep part of the brain called the striatum while rats learned routes like this one.

teach.h: BUSY AT THE EDGES, QUIET IN THE MIDDLE.
teach.b: Early on, that region was busy all through the run, as if the rat were working out each step. Second, the change.
As the route became a habit, the activity bunched up at the edges: a burst at the start, when the click sounded and the gate opened, and another at the end, near the reward. The middle went quieter.
The whole run had become one packaged chunk. Third, the loop.
A popular book by journalist Charles Duhigg turned findings like these into three words: cue, routine, reward.
The cue is the trigger, the routine is the packaged behavior, the reward is what makes the brain want to run it again. A phone buzzes, the hand reaches, a little news arrives. Fourth, a fair warning.
The three-word loop is a handy map, not a law of nature. The lab work is messier, and real habits tangle together.
But the map points somewhere useful. If the burst of activity sits at the start, the start is where a habit is easiest to see. Once the routine is running, it's on rails.
Before it runs, there's a click. Learning to spot that moment is the beginning of having a say in what follows.

how: People working on a habit sometimes write down one loop they repeat, naming the cue that starts it, the routine itself and the reward it brings, as a first step before trying to change anything.

o: the signal that sets off a habit's routine
the reward that comes at the end of a habit
the routine itself, once it runs on its own

games.q: you want to understand one of your own habits. where do you look first?
o: the middle of the routine, once it's running.
the cue, the moment before it starts.
games.why: the lab saw bursts of activity at the start of the habit. the cue is where a habit is easiest to see.

practice: Rest on the breath, and as small signals arrive, an itch, a sound outside, a sudden thought of something undone, treat each one as a click, a gate sliding open.
Notice the pull that follows, name it quietly, "cue," and stay where you are for one more breath. You don't have to fight the urge; just watch the moment between the click and the run.

wordCard.voice: Cue. The signal at the start of a habit loop, where the lab saw a burst of activity, and where a habit is easiest to see. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the cue is where a habit can be seen. The click comes first, and it's the easiest part to catch. See you tomorrow.
